analysis.one_liner: Requires political ads to disclose when images or video are AI-generated.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to label AI-generated political ads was referred to committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any political ad that contains an image or video made with artificial intelligence to clearly state that fact — in writing, in the audio, or on screen depending on the format. It would also extend existing campaign-ad rules to paid online ads on large platforms, requiring them to report those ads to the Federal Election Commission, and direct the FEC to write rules defining what counts as AI-generated content. The bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would know when a face, voice, or scene in a political ad was generated by AI rather than being real. It also gives campaigns and outside groups the same clear rules, and gives the FEC data on who is paying for online political ads.

how_it_helps.text: Any political ad containing an image or video footage generated in whole or in part by AI must carry a clear, conspicuous statement saying so, with specific format rules for text, audio, and video ads.

The Federal Election Commission must issue rules defining AI-generated content and criteria for spotting it, and must report to Congress every two years on compliance and on further ways to bring transparency to political ads.

The bill extends existing 'electioneering communication' disclosure rules to paid online and digital ads on large platforms, closing a gap where TV and radio ads had disclosure requirements but paid internet ads generally did not.

analysis.who_pays: Political campaigns, parties, and outside groups running AI-assisted ads would bear the cost of adding disclaimers, and large online platforms and ad vendors would take on new reporting and compliance work for paid political ads.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only image and video content generated by AI — it does not require disclosure for AI-generated voices or text alone, so some synthetic content would still go unlabeled.
The disclosure requirement applies only to ads on 'online platforms' with 50 million or more monthly U.S. visitors, so paid political ads on smaller sites and apps would escape the new online rules.

It adds compliance costs for campaigns and ad agencies, and requires the FEC to draw a line around fast-changing AI technology, which could produce burdensome or inconsistent determinations for small advertisers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to voters — knowing when political ads show fabricated images or video — is real and cheap to provide: a label in the ad. The costs fall on advertisers and large platforms as compliance work, not on the public. The main honest criticism is that the bill is narrower than the problem: it skips AI voices and text and only covers large platforms, so a motivated bad actor has routes around it. Still, it is a targeted disclosure rule whose costs are modest and whose main burden falls on people running the ads, not on ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was assigned to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it never reached a vote in the Senate.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 15, 2023, joined by Sens. Cory Booker and Michael Bennet.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration, where it remained.
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Campaigns, outside groups, and large digital platforms are better off: they can continue running paid online political ads, including AI-generated imagery, with no federal requirement to label AI content or report those ads to the FEC.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ad buyers and large online platforms

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill never advanced to a vote where partisan lines could have been measured.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and digital ad vendors
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users would have to process AI disclaimers on political ads and report paid political communications to the FEC. Many already follow similar disclosure rules voluntarily, so the added cost is compliance work — but the rules also raise the barrier to running cheap, unlabeled AI ads, which some ad buyers would prefer to avoid.

industries.industry: Political campaigns and outside spending groups
industries.note: Campaigns gain clear legal rules and the ability to use AI tools openly with a disclaimer, but they lose the option of using synthetic images and video without telling viewers. The cost is small relative to ad budgets.

industries.industry: AI content generation tools and agencies serving political clients
industries.note: Firms selling AI-generated images and video to political clients would face clients who must disclose the use, which could dampen demand for unlabeled synthetic political content. The bill does not restrict the technology itself.
